blocks.html:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Understanding climate change

Are the climatic changes the world is seeing now really unprecedented, or have there been other times when change was just as swift? ‘If we go back to the past and find there really hasn’t been anything like this before, then that strengthens the case that human activity is responsible for the rapid changes we are seeing today,’ says climatologist Dennis Wheeler of the University of Sunderland, UK.

But the past is tricky territory for climatologists. While tree rings and ice cores chart annual changes in climate going back millennia, they cannot show what happened on a month-to-month basis. There are some long-running chronicles of temperature and air pressure over land dating back to the 17th century, but systematic records of air movements over the oceans — which govern most of our weather — were almost non-existent before the mid-19th century, by which time the Industrial Revolution was already well under way, and factory chimneys were pouring carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. In order to establish whether today’s climate changes indeed had any precedent in the past, what Wheeler needed was detailed information from earlier times, and he soon became convinced that the multitude of jottings in old ships’ records could provide just that.

By the late 17th century, the seafaring nations of Europe had fleets of ships criss-crossing the seas, all keeping meticulous accounts of their voyages, including regular observations of weather conditions. In 1731, it became obligatory for British naval vessels to keep a detailed logbook, and by 1750 the practice was universal. A vast number of such records survive to this day. Despite initial reluctance among climatologists to use these historical documents for scientific research, Wheeler and his team secured funding for a project to sift through two thousand old logbooks. They pored over records of English, Dutch, French and Spanish fleets, with the aim of creating a climatological database for the world’s oceans between 1750 and 1850.

In order to reconstruct air pressure fields as they move across the sea, climate ‘modellers’ need details of wind strength and direction at as many locations as possible. The team’s research produced the equivalent of two million days of information but, plentiful as this data was, much of it needed translation. Until 1805, even a day wasn’t a day as we know it, but a nautical day, which started at noon. Before 1752, the year began on 25 March, and until September of that year the English calendar lagged 10 days behind the one used in the rest of Europe.

Even the wind’s direction posed a problem. It took a long time to work out if the direction noted in the log was based on magnetic north or true north. Get it wrong and the data could be out by as much as 30 degrees. ‘On British vessels, most observations were magnetic. Once a day, officers would convert the readings to true north — but the logbooks don’t tell you that,’ says Wheeler. ‘It took some detective work to find out what was going on.’

Harder still was interpreting observations on the strength of the wind. It was 1850 before most ships were equipped with accurate instruments to collect climatic data, previous to which officers had to rely on judgement and experience. And, as the numerical Beaufort scale of wind strength did not become official until 1838, most of the logbooks in Wheeler’s archives describe weather conditions using words alone — and often archaic or peculiar ones. A sample of English logs from 1685 to 1700 produced 73 different ways of describing the wind’s force. To everyone’s relief, closer scrutiny showed that many terms were used just once or twice: most log-keepers stuck to a similar set of terms.

So how strong was a wind described as ‘moderate’, or a gale described as ‘fine’? And did all seafarers have the same thing in mind when they used them? This was tested by checking how far the ships sailed each day, another fact carefully recorded in the logbook. The speed a sailing ship travelled was directly linked to the force of the wind, at least up to Beaufort force 7. ‘If you have a large enough sample you can pick out all the days when officers described, for example, a “fine breeze”, and check the sea-miles covered,’ says Wheeler. ‘That gives a measure of the relative wind strength.’

Having to deal with logs from four nations, from both naval and merchant vessels, made the task of translating archaic terms into hard numbers doubly daunting. Toughest of all was unravelling the terms used aboard trading ships. These had their own complex vocabulary of gales, trade winds, and monsoons, each in several grades, Wheeler discovered. But, by checking sea-miles covered, and cross-checking with the logs of occasional naval escorts, the team eventually worked out which terms meant what. Pairs of ships in convoy, or squadrons in the same locality, should have the same records, so allowing the researchers to check for consistency.

The wealth of data Wheeler was able to call on enabled him to show statistically that the expressions used in the logbooks were not vague approximations, but precise terms falling into distinct categories. The researchers have now fitted nearly all the terms used into the Beaufort scale, and have high hopes that the seafarers of the pre-instrumental age will, in time, give today’s scientists a valuable insight into the causes of global climate change.

questionGroups.bodyHtml:
Questions 14–17

Complete the summary. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the text for each answer.

Why look at old ships’ logbooks?

Dennis Wheeler of the University of Sunderland set out to determine to what extent is changing the climate of our planet. Scientific evidence of past climate changes, such as wood specimens or samples cut from ice, were of little use for Wheeler’s investigations because these materials provided no indication of changing conditions from one to the next.

Wheeler’s research called for a large number of highly detailed daily reports on atmospheric conditions occurring over the world’s . These reports also needed to date from a period before the , which was, by the middle of the nineteenth century, already causing widespread atmospheric pollution.

Questions 18–21

Complete the table. Write ONE YEAR from the text for each answer.

Year
The keeping of logbooks was made compulsory on British naval ships.
The system of dates was standardised across Europe.
Ships’ logbooks ceased the practice of starting each day’s record at midday.
A definitive scale of recording wind force was adopted.
Most ships had been equipped with reliable weather-recording instruments.1850

Questions 22–23

Choose TWO correct answers.

Which TWO problems are mentioned in the passage?

Questions 24–26

Do the following statements agree with the information given in the text?

  • TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
  • FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
  • NOT GIVEN if there is no information about this

24. The earliest extensive weather records still in existence date from the 19th century.

25. The relationship between wind speed and distance sailed was used to aid interpretation of descriptive vocabulary.

26. Comparisons were made between the logbooks of different vessels sailing in the same area.

items.text:
（1）题目 14：
题目翻译：Dennis Wheeler 希望确定，________ 在多大程度上正在改变地球气候。
答案：human activity
定位：第1段，第2句
原文：human activity is responsible for the rapid changes we are seeing today
译文：人类活动应对我们今天看到的快速变化负责。

解析：题干的 is changing the climate 对应原文 is responsible for the rapid changes。原文把造成当今快速变化的因素明确指向 human activity，因此答案为 human activity。

（2）题目 15：
题目翻译：这些材料无法显示从一个 ________ 到下一个时段之间的条件变化。
答案：month
定位：第2段，第2句
原文：they cannot show what happened on a month-to-month basis
译文：它们无法显示逐月发生的情况。

解析：题干 from one ... to the next 改写原文 month-to-month。空格需要填入单数时间单位 month，补回后形成 from one month to the next。

（3）题目 16：
题目翻译：Wheeler 的研究需要关于世界各地 ________ 上空气象状况的大量详细逐日报告。
答案：oceans
定位：第2段，第3句
原文：systematic records of air movements over the oceans
译文：海洋上空空气流动的系统记录。

解析：题干 atmospheric conditions occurring over 对应原文 air movements over；空格前的 world’s 与原文 the oceans 共同指向全球海洋，因此答案用原文复数 oceans。

（4）题目 17：
题目翻译：这些报告还必须来自 ________ 之前；到19世纪中叶，这一事件已经造成广泛的大气污染。
答案：Industrial Revolution
定位：第2段，第3句
原文：by which time the Industrial Revolution was already well under way, and factory chimneys were pouring carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
译文：到那时，工业革命已经全面展开，工厂烟囱正把二氧化碳排入大气。

解析：原文说明到了19世纪中叶，Industrial Revolution 已全面展开，工厂烟囱正在向大气排放二氧化碳。题干 before the ... 与这段时间和污染信息对应，所以答案是完整专名 Industrial Revolution。

items.text:
（1）题目 18：________
题目翻译：表格：英国海军舰船被强制要求保留航海日志——年份：________。
答案：1731
定位：第3段，第2句
原文：In 1731, it became obligatory for British naval vessels to keep a detailed logbook
译文：1731年，英国海军舰船被规定必须保留详细的航海日志。

解析：表格中的 made compulsory 对应原文 became obligatory。原文直接给出该规定开始的年份 1731。

（2）题目 19：________
题目翻译：表格：欧洲各地的日期制度实现统一——年份：________。
答案：1752
定位：第4段，末句
原文：Before 1752, the year began on 25 March, and until September of that year the English calendar lagged 10 days behind the one used in the rest of Europe.
译文：1752年以前，一年从3月25日开始；直到该年9月，英国历法仍比欧洲其他地区所用历法晚10天。

解析：原文说 1752 年以前英国历法仍与欧洲其他地区不同，并一直到该年9月还落后10天。因此表格要求的制度统一年份是 1752。

（3）题目 20：________
题目翻译：表格：航海日志停止把正午作为每日记录的起点——年份：________。
答案：1805
定位：第4段，第3句
原文：Until 1805, even a day wasn’t a day as we know it, but a nautical day, which started at noon.
译文：直到1805年，一天仍不是我们今天理解的一天，而是从正午开始的航海日。

解析：原文 Until 1805 表示从正午开始的 nautical day 做法一直持续到 1805 年；题干 ceased the practice 对应这一时间界限。

（4）题目 21：________
题目翻译：表格：记录风力的正式标准被采用——年份：________。
答案：1838
定位：第6段，第3句
原文：the numerical Beaufort scale of wind strength did not become official until 1838
译文：数字化的蒲福风力等级直到1838年才成为正式标准。

解析：题干 definitive scale was adopted 对应原文 numerical Beaufort scale became official。原文直接给出的正式采用年份是 1838；1850 对应大多数船只已配备可靠仪器的另一时间节点。

items.text:
（1）题目 22：
题目翻译：以下列出了一些解读早期航海日志时可能遇到的问题。文章提到了其中哪两项？
答案：C（non-numerical descriptions of wind force）
定位：第6段，第3句
原文：most of the logbooks in Wheeler’s archives describe weather conditions using words alone — and often archaic or peculiar ones
译文：Wheeler 档案中的大多数航海日志只用文字描述天气状况，而且常常使用古老或特殊的词语。

解析：原文明确说明早期日志没有统一数值尺度，风力主要用文字描述，正对应“风力的非数字化描述”。因此这是两个正确问题之一。

（2）题目 23：
题目翻译：以下列出了一些解读早期航海日志时可能遇到的问题。文章提到了其中哪两项？
答案：E（variations in terminology used by different sailing professions）
定位：第8段，第1—3句
原文：Having to deal with logs from four nations, from both naval and merchant vessels, made the task of translating archaic terms into hard numbers doubly daunting. Toughest of all was unravelling the terms used aboard trading ships. These had their own complex vocabulary of gales, trade winds, and monsoons, each in several grades, Wheeler discovered.
译文：研究人员需要处理来自四个国家、海军舰船和商船的日志，这使得把古老术语转换为具体数值的任务更加艰巨。最困难的是弄清商船使用的术语；Wheeler 发现，它们有自己复杂的词汇来描述大风、信风和季风，而且每种还分成若干等级。

解析：海军舰船和商船使用的术语存在差异，商船还有自己复杂的分级词汇，对应 E 所说的不同航海职业使用不同术语。第5段只说误判磁北与真北可能导致偏差，并未说日志中已发现风向记录错误，不能据此选择 D。因此两项正确答案为 C 和 E。

items.text:
（1）题目 24：The earliest extensive weather records still in existence date from the 19th century.
题目翻译：现存最早的大规模天气记录始于19世纪。
答案：FALSE
定位：第2段，第3句
原文：There are some long-running chronicles of temperature and air pressure over land dating back to the 17th century
译文：有些长期记录陆地温度和气压的资料可以追溯到17世纪。

解析：题干称最早记录始于19世纪，但原文明确说已有记录可追溯到17世纪，时间直接矛盾，因此答案为 FALSE。

（2）题目 25：The relationship between wind speed and distance sailed was used to aid interpretation of descriptive vocabulary.
题目翻译：研究人员利用风速与航行距离的关系来帮助解释描述性词汇。
答案：TRUE
定位：第7段，第3—4句
原文：This was tested by checking how far the ships sailed each day, another fact carefully recorded in the logbook. The speed a sailing ship travelled was directly linked to the force of the wind, at least up to Beaufort force 7.
译文：研究人员通过核查船只每天航行多远来进行检验；帆船速度与风力直接相关，至少在蒲福风力7级以内如此。

解析：原文把每日航行距离与风力强弱直接联系起来，并用这种关系校准 fine breeze 等描述性词汇。题干准确概括了方法，因此答案为 TRUE。

（3）题目 26：Comparisons were made between the logbooks of different vessels sailing in the same area.
题目翻译：研究人员比较了同一地区航行的不同船只的航海日志。
答案：TRUE
定位：第8段，末两句
原文：But, by checking sea-miles covered, and cross-checking with the logs of occasional naval escorts, the team eventually worked out which terms meant what. Pairs of ships in convoy, or squadrons in the same locality, should have the same records, so allowing the researchers to check for consistency.
译文：团队通过核查航行里程，并与偶尔护航的海军舰船日志交叉比对，最终弄清了词语含义；同一船队或同一地点的舰队理应有相同记录，这使研究人员能够检查一致性。

解析：cross-checking 明确表明研究人员比较了不同船只的日志；in the same locality 又与题干 sailing in the same area 对应，所以答案为 TRUE，而不是 NOT GIVEN。

定位：第8段，末两句
原文：But, by checking sea-miles covered, and cross-checking with the logs of occasional naval escorts, the team eventually worked out which terms meant what. Pairs of ships in convoy, or squadrons in the same locality, should have the same records, so allowing the researchers to check for consistency.
译文：团队通过核查航行里程，并与偶尔护航的海军舰船日志交叉比对，最终弄清了词语含义；同一船队或同一地点的舰队理应有相同记录，这使研究人员能够检查一致性。

解析：cross-checking 明确表明研究人员比较了不同船只的日志；in the same locality 又与题干 sailing in the same area 对应，所以答案为 TRUE，而不是 NOT GIVEN。
